articles.headline: OFAC Removes Venezuela-Related Designation
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a Venezuela-related designation removal on October 14, 2026. This action is part of ongoing adjustments to the sanctions program concerning Venezuela.

This removal follows previous guidance from OFAC indicating that, absent progress towards a free and competitive 2024 presidential election, General License (GL) 44, which authorized transactions related to oil and gas sector operations in Venezuela, would not be renewed upon its expiration in April 2024.

The revocation of GL 43, which authorized transactions involving CVG Compania General de Mineria de Venezuela CA, also preceded this removal, effectively snapping back sanctions on the Venezuelan oil and mining sectors.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Entities for Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations on October 13, 2026, targeting entities involved in counter narcotics and counter terrorism activities. These actions aim to disrupt illicit financial networks supporting such operations globally.

These designations underscore the U.S. government's continued efforts to combat international drug trafficking and terrorist financing by identifying and sanctioning individuals and entities that facilitate these illicit activities.

The specific details of the designated entities and the nature of their involvement were not immediately available in the initial announcement, but such designations typically result in the blocking of assets and prohibitions on transactions with U.S. persons.

articles.headline: Bank of America Settles with OFAC for Sanctions Violations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a settlement agreement with Bank of America, N.A. on October 13, 2026, for apparent violations of numerous sanctions programs.

Bank of America agreed to a settlement of $11,662,930 for 475 apparent violations, which occurred when the bank channeled correspondent banking payments through blocked banks due to technical and human error, allowed designated individuals to make payments and withdraw funds due to poor sanctions alert calibration, failed to promptly update watchlists, and mishandled business accounts associated with blocked persons.

These compliance failures resulted in Bank of America processing millions of dollars in payments in apparent violation of sanctions programs targeting Russia, Belarus, Iran, Burma, Somalia, narcotics, and global terrorism. The settlement amount reflects OFAC's determination that the violations were non-egregious and largely not voluntarily self-disclosed, with no reduction for remedial measures or cooperation.

articles.headline: OFAC Announces Settlement with Pegasus Worldwide Logistics, ICC Designation, and Burma-Related Removal
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a settlement agreement with Pegasus Worldwide Logistics on October 9, 2026. Concurrently, OFAC issued an International Criminal Court (ICC) designation and a Burma-related designation removal.

The settlement with Pegasus Worldwide Logistics addresses apparent violations of OFAC sanctions regulations, the specifics of which were not detailed in the initial announcement but are typically related to unauthorized transactions or dealings with sanctioned entities.
The ICC designation and Burma-related removal reflect the dynamic nature of U.S. sanctions policy, adapting to geopolitical developments and specific foreign policy objectives.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues New Russia-Related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued a new Russia-related General License (GL) on October 9, 2026. This GL authorizes certain transactions that would otherwise be prohibited under the Russia sanctions program.

General Licenses are frequently issued to provide clarity and allow for specific types of transactions that are deemed necessary or consistent with U.S. foreign policy objectives, even within a sanctioned environment.
The details of the newly issued GL specify the scope of authorized activities, providing guidance to U.S. persons and entities on permissible engagements related to Russia.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Iran-Related Designations, Issues New and Amended General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on October 8, 2026, alongside the issuance of a new Iran-related General License and an amended Russia-related General License.

These actions are part of ongoing efforts to exert pressure on Iran while providing specific authorizations for certain activities. The amended Russia-related General License indicates adjustments to existing sanctions to address evolving circumstances.

The new Iran-related General License aims to facilitate certain humanitarian or other permissible transactions, while the designations target entities or individuals deemed to be supporting Iran's illicit activities.

articles.headline: OFAC Publishes Iran-Related Alert and Amended FAQ, Announces Designations Removals and Updates
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) published an Iran-related Alert and an amended Iran-related Frequently Asked Question (FAQ) on October 5, 2026. Concurrently, OFAC announced several designations removals and updates.

The Alert warns foreign financial institutions (FFIs) that continuing to transact with sanctioned Iranian financial institutions could result in being targeted at any time without advance notification. This marks a shift from previous guidance where OFAC generally contacted FFIs before making such a finding.

The amended FAQ 156 clarifies how an FFI will be informed of OFAC's finding regarding sanctionable activity. These actions are part of 'Operation Economic Outcast,' launched in August 2026, to cut off financial resources supporting the Iranian regime.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Counter Terrorism Designations on October 2, 2026. These designations target individuals and entities involved in supporting terrorist activities globally.
These actions are part of the U.S. government's ongoing commitment to disrupt the financial networks of terrorist organizations and prevent them from accessing the international financial system.
The specific details of the designated parties were not immediately available, but such designations typically result in the freezing of assets and prohibitions on transactions with U.S. persons.

articles.headline: OFAC Announces Iran-Related Designations and Updates, Transnational Criminal Organizations Designation
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations and designations updates on October 1, 2026. Additionally, OFAC issued a Transnational Criminal Organizations designation, and published an Iran-related Determination and an amended Iran-related Frequently Asked Question.

These actions signify a continued focus on Iran's illicit activities and the networks that support them, including those involved in transnational criminal enterprises. The determination and amended FAQ provide further guidance on the scope and application of Iran sanctions.
The designations aim to disrupt financial flows and other support for the Iranian regime and criminal organizations, reinforcing the U.S. government's commitment to countering these threats.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Counter Terrorism and Transnational Criminal Organizations, Removes Belarus, Narcotics, and Libya Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations targeting Counter Terrorism and Transnational Criminal Organizations on September 30, 2026. Concurrently, OFAC issued designations removals related to Belarus, Counter Narcotics, and Libya.

These actions reflect a dual approach of targeting ongoing threats from terrorism and criminal organizations while also adjusting sanctions regimes in response to evolving geopolitical landscapes and policy considerations.

The removals of designations for Belarus, Counter Narcotics, and Libya indicate a reassessment of the necessity or effectiveness of those specific sanctions, potentially signaling shifts in diplomatic or enforcement strategies.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Implementation of EAR Export Controls on Silencers, Mufflers, and Sound Suppressors; and Other Firearms Related Changes
body: The Department of Commerce (Commerce), Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is revising the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Commerce Control List (CCL) to appropriately control certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors (sound suppressors) that will no longer be described on the International Traffic in Arms Regulations U.S. Munitions List (USML). This interim final rule (IFR) complements a Department of State interim final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register (International Traffic in Arms Regulations: USML Category I Firearm Suppressors (1400-AG11) (State IFR)). This transfer of jurisdiction will reduce the regulatory burden on exports of sound suppressors. This IFR also revises the EAR to allow firearms and related items to be temporarily exported and reexported under a license exception as tools of trade, thereby relieving exporters of the regulatory burden of applying for authorization. Finally, this IFR clarifies which items fall within the scope of the EAR's entry clearance requirements for a temporary import.

articles.headline: Enhanced Favorable Treatment for the United Arab Emirates Under the Export Administration Regulations
body: In this final rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to provide enhanced favorable treatment for the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Specifically, BIS is removing the UAE from Country Groups D:3 and D:4 and adding the UAE to Country Group A:5. More license exceptions will now be available, including Strategic Trade Authorization (STA) for the UAE Government and approved commercial entities in the UAE. STA will authorize the export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) of military items; certain commercial satellites and spacecraft; and dual-use items useful in, inter alia, oil and gas production, desalination, and civil nuclear power generation. The UAE Government and approved commercial entities will also have license-free access to advanced computing items, consistent with the May 2025 U.S.-UAE Artificial Intelligence Cooperation framework, without compromising U.S. digital infrastructure buildout.
